title_original: Paris Photo 2026 : Proyectos Monclova Gallery : Kati Horna

blocks.text: Proyectos Monclova Gallery (Booth #D38) announces its debut presentation at Paris Photo , on view at the Grand Palais , with a solo booth devoted to Hungarian-born Mexican photographer Kati Horna (1912 – 2000). This follows the gallery’s recent announcement of exclusive representation of the Estate of Kati Horna and marks the first time the gallery has dedicated its participation in an international photography fair to the work of a single artist. A retrospective of Kati Horna, curated by Daniel Garza Usabiaga, is now on view at the Museo del Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City through February 7, 2027.

Born in Szilasbalhás, Hungary, Horna settled in Mexico after the outbreak of the Second World War. She resided in Mexico until her death, producing a fundamental part of her work there. The presentation traces various stages of Horna’s career—from her years in Paris in the 1930s to her portraits of artists made in Mexico and her collaborations with the magazine S.nob in the 1960s—and reveals how she developed the modernist eye that earned her a significant place in avant-garde photography.

Horna arrived in Paris in 1933 and during her early years in the city would produce the series Marchés aux puces (Flea Markets) and Cafés de París (Paris Cafés) , works from which will be on view at the booth. Flea markets also drew other foreign photographers working in the city, such as André Kertész, Brassaï and Germaine Krull; in the streets and cafés of Paris, Horna captured everyday life and the city’s spaces of leisure, with a singular ability to find humor and intimacy in the ordinary.

The booth will also reflect a selection of works developed in Mexico City, following Horna’s move there in 1939. In Mexico City, Horna and her husband, the Spanish artist José Horna, became part of a community of exiled European artists and intellectuals. Portraits of two central figures of that circle, the English painter Leonora Carrington and the Spanish artist Remedios Varo, with whom Horna shared close personal and creative bonds, will figure on the booth.

Also featured are two series made for the “Fetiches” section of S.nob , the magazine founded by Salvador Elizondo, Juan García Ponce and Emilio García Riera. Oda a la necrofilia (Ode to Necrophilia) , published in the first issue, was conceived as a staged scene in collaboration with Leonora Carrington: a woman dressed in black, her face hidden beneath a veil, embodies death. In Paraísos artificiales (Artificial Paradises) , for which cultural promoter Luz del Amo posed, the uncanny emerges from the meeting of the living and the inanimate, the sinister and the familiar.

Further emphasizing Horna’s collaborations with Leonora Carrington will be works from the series Mujer y máscara (Woman and Mask) . Mujer y máscara was made for Mexico This Month , the magazine edited by Anita Brenner to which Horna contributed between 1958 and 1965. The mask that appears in Horna’s images was made by Leonora Carrington.

With this selection, Proyectos Monclova Gallery highlights Kati Horna’s significance for the history of photography in Mexico and for the country’s artistic avant-gardes through a practice that moved between documentary, portraiture, experimentation and staged photography.

Kati Horna (b. Szilasbalhás (now Mezőszilas), Hungary, 1912, d. Mexico City, 2000) was a Hungarian-born avant-garde photographer and a seminal figure in twentieth-century photography in Mexico. Her career unfolded across Hungary, Germany, France, Spain, and, above all, Mexico, where she settled and lived for much of her life. Her photographic practice encompassed a wide range of genres, including war photojournalism, documentary and street photography, portraiture, and architectural photography—reflecting both her political convictions and her interest in the encounter between the everyday and the fantastic. She also developed avant-garde artistic approaches through experimentation with photographic materials, the use of photomontage, and a visual language associated with Surrealism. She is considered one of the most important figures of the Surrealist Photography movement in the country, alongside Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo.

Her work in Mexico coincided with the beginning of a long period of economic expansion and urban growth in the country, and she quickly became involved with the graphic press in Mexico City, with which she collaborated until the end of her career. Among the numerous Mexican publications for which she worked were Nosotros, Tiempo, Mujeres: Expresión femenina, Revista de la Universidad de México, Arquitectura México, Mexico This Month, and Diseño. Her photographic production reveals the rapid transformation of the city and its vibrant cultural life in the mid-twentieth century.

Established in 2005, Proyectos Monclova is a leading contemporary art gallery based in Mexico City. The gallery represents a roster of some of Mexico’s most acclaimed contemporary artists, including young and mid-career artists, alongside established great masters. In 2010, the gallery sought to bolster its programming by bringing in international artists, further enriching its dialogue.

Proyectos Monclova has become a vital force within the Mexican art world, playing a critical role in expanding Mexico’s presence on the global art scene and participating in numerous prestigious international art fairs. The gallery continues to advance its mission by offering a dynamic program that enriches both local and international discourse through notable exhibitions, institutional collaborations, artist initiatives, and scholarly publications.
Paris Photo Nov. 12–15, 2026 | Grand Palais 1 pm – 8 pm (Sunday 7 pm) Avenue Winston Churchill 75008, Paris, France Booth P01 www.parisphoto.com
